title: How To Handle A Student Whose Grades (And Behavior) Have Dropped
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues against the common teacher reflex of immediately pulling aside a student whose grades or behavior have started slipping, contending that premature intervention interferes with a student's ability to work through struggles on their own and can foster learned helplessness. He recommends waiting roughly a week, depending on grade level, before stepping in, so students have the chance to build resilience by 'fighting through' on their own. If a week passes without improvement, he suggests a single simple, open-ended question—'I notice you're not doing as well lately. Are you okay?'—rather than lectures or advice. He is careful to carve out an exception for any suspicion of bullying, trauma, or danger, which warrants immediate action, but argues that in most ordinary cases, patience builds more lasting confidence than quick intervention.
points: Argues premature intervention when a student struggles can foster learned helplessness rather than resilience.
Recommends waiting roughly a week, depending on grade level, before addressing a noticeable drop in grades or behavior.
Suggests a single open-ended question—'I notice you're not doing as well lately. Are you okay?'—rather than lectures.
Carves out an explicit exception: any suspicion of bullying, trauma, or danger warrants immediate intervention.
Frames the goal as impacting students for a lifetime, not just getting them through the current day or school year.
quotes: The reason is that it prevents students from fighting through and overcoming trials and tribulations all on their own, which is infinitely more instructive.
When a student through grit and determination is able to rejoin the peloton of their own accord it makes them more resilient.
It extinguishes their intrinsic desire to improve and change their life circumstances—which is a trait the happiest, most successful people share and that many of our students are in short supply.

It’s important to note that if at any time you suspect bullying, trauma, homelessness, mental health issues, etc. or that they’re in a potentially dangerous situation, you must always and immediately step in.
It provides the tools we all need to survive, reverse course, and thrive in the end.
